newsitem.title: FRANCE: French recognition for Spanish Civil War vets.
newsitem.headline: French recognition for Spanish Civil War vets.

text.p: France's parliament on Thursday voted to extend official recognition, including small pensions, to the few French survivors of the International Brigades which fought with the Republicans in the 1936-1939 Spanish Civil War.

The National Assembly accepted an amendment extending the statutory rights of an "ancien combattant" (war veteran) to an estimated 200 surviving Brigades members whose fighting record now will be officially recognised as services to France itself.

The move, which had been in and out of parliament for years, was given a final push by President Jacques Chirac who wanted it to coincide with a November 23 national tribute to French writer and long-time cultural affairs minister Andre Malraux, who led an international air squadron in the Spanish War.
Sympathisers of the veterans long campaigned for official recognition for them on grounds they were pioneers in the fight against fascism before France itself was occupied by Nazi Germany in 1940.
The move was resisted by some conservatives on grounds that the Brigades, which last month celebrated in Spain the 60th anniversary of their creation, were heavily influenced by the Soviet Union.

France, which discreetly aided the Republicans against the insurgent right-wing nationalists led by General Francisco Franco, who went on to rule Spain until his death in 1975, officially stayed out of the Spanish War.
Around 35,000 men and women from 53 countries fought in the International Brigades, suffering 10,000 dead and earning a place in the pantheon of left-wing heroes.
The French were the single largest national contingent, supplying 9,000 volunteers of whom about a third were killed in Spain with an equal number later dying during World War Two.
While half the French volunteers were non-communists, the Brigades' leadership was overwhelmingly communist.
